name: Enter bills of lading as freight bills
summary: Every LTL shipment starts as a paper or electronic bill of lading signed at the shipper's dock. Each evening terminal clerks scan the paper bills and central billing clerks key them into the transportation management system, or check the electronic ones, so that a freight bill exists before linehaul planners build the night's trailers and before the rating engine prices it. About 60% of bills are still paper in 2019-2022, many handwritten, so the work is a high-volume keying job against a hard overnight cut-off. Illegible addresses, missing bill-to parties and wrong freight classes cause queries the same night and rebills weeks later.

baseline.org_archetype: A Canadian LTL and truckload carrier of about 3,000 employees with 38 terminals, five hubs and a central billing centre that keys bills of lading from images on an evening shift.
baseline.notes: The workflow starts when the city driver's paperwork reaches the terminal and ends when the freight bill is released and matched to the dock loading scans. Signing the bill at the shipper belongs to pickup execution; pricing belongs to rating and invoicing.

trigger: A city driver hands in the signed bill of lading at the end of the route, or the shipper's electronic bill arrives and its signed paper copy is scanned.
end_state: A complete freight bill is released in the TMS and matched to the dock loading scans, or the bill is voided as a duplicate.

volume.seasonality: Lowest in January and in April-May 2020 during COVID-19 lockdowns; highest from September to mid-December. Mondays and the day after a holiday carry about 20% more bills than other weekdays.

evidence.note: Equal to the organisation file's LTL shipments driver (one bill of lading per shipment); author's estimate.

surge.cause: Autumn shipping peak (September to mid-December retail and industrial restocking)

evidence.note: Taken from the organisation file's process entry; LTL volumes in Canada rise from September to early December.

Duties from a US LTL rate clerk posting. FTE: about 1.7 hands-on minutes per bill times 150,000 bills is about 33 FTE at 130 productive hours; 33 of the organisation file's 45 billing clerks are assigned here, the rest to rating.
Supervises the evening keying shift, audits samples and handles system faults; author's estimate.
Scanning, envelope checks and answering billing queries take about 1.1 minutes per bill across 38 terminals, about 18 FTE of the 45 terminal service clerks; author's estimate.

systems.name: Transportation management system (LTL and truckload operations, billing, rating)
Document imaging for bills of lading and delivery receipts
EDI gateway (204 tenders, 211 bills of lading, 214 status, 210 invoices)
Customer web portal (pickup requests, tracing, documents)
Email, phone system and contact centre software

steps.name: Check driver paperwork against pickup list
steps.description: When a city driver returns from the route, the terminal service clerk opens the driver's envelope and checks that every pickup on the route manifest has a signed bill of lading with a PRO label attached. Missing bills are listed against the driver and the shipper.

error.defect_description: A bill is put in the wrong terminal batch or left in the envelope.

next.condition: a bill of lading is missing

evidence.note: Common practice: drivers hand in bills at the end of the route; 2% missing is the author's estimate.

steps.name: Request a copy of a missing bill of lading
steps.description: The terminal service clerk calls the driver and, if the driver does not have it, the shipper's shipping office to ask for a copy of the signed bill of lading by fax or email. The pickup stays open on the missing-paperwork list until the copy arrives.

error.defect_description: None introduced; errors pass through.

evidence.note: Author's estimate of the call and email time.

steps.name: Shipper or driver supplies the copy
steps.description: The shipper's shipping office finds its copy of the bill of lading and faxes or emails it, or the driver finds it in the truck on the next shift. Copies often arrive the next morning when the shipper's office opens.

error.defect_description: None introduced; errors pass through.

evidence.note: Shipper offices work day hours; an evening request is usually answered next morning. Author's estimate.

steps.name: Scan bills of lading into imaging
steps.description: The terminal service clerk feeds the stack of bills of lading through the document scanner in batches. Each page is imaged and sent to the central billing queue, where the PRO barcode label identifies the shipment.

error.defect_description: Page skipped, skewed or unreadable image.

evidence.note: Common practice at LTL carriers with central billing; author's estimate of scanning time per page.

steps.name: Index image by PRO number and match electronic bill
steps.description: The imaging system reads the PRO barcode, attaches the image to the shipment record and checks whether the shipper already sent the same bill electronically by EDI 211 or through the customer portal. Matched bills go to automatic creation; the rest go to the keying queue.

error.defect_description: Barcode misread links the image to the wrong PRO.

evidence.note: The 211 transaction carries the legal bill of lading electronically; the 40% electronic share is the author's estimate for a Canadian LTL carrier in 2019-2022.

steps.name: Report imaging or EDI fault to the IT service desk
steps.description: When the image queue stops filling or EDI bills stop arriving, the billing supervisor raises a ticket with the IT service desk, tells the terminals to send images by email and moves the affected bills to manual keying so the night's cut-off is met.

error.defect_description: None introduced; errors pass through.

evidence.note: Author's estimate; faults are rare but each one affects a batch of bills.

steps.name: Build freight bill from the electronic bill of lading
steps.description: The TMS creates the freight bill from the EDI 211 or portal data and runs edits: valid shipper and consignee codes, bill-to party, postal codes in the service area, pieces and weight present, freight class or dimensions present and dangerous goods flags consistent.

error.defect_description: Shipper sent data that differs from the signed paper bill (pieces, weight or consignee).

evidence.note: 211 data carries quantity, weight and classification; 15% edit failure is the author's estimate.

steps.name: Correct electronic bills that fail edits
steps.description: A billing clerk opens the failed electronic bill beside the signed paper image, corrects the consignee address, bill-to party or missing class, and keeps the signed paper figures where the two disagree because the signed bill is the contract of carriage.

error.defect_description: Clerk accepts the EDI figure where the paper bill differs.

evidence.note: Author's estimate of correction time.

steps.name: Key the freight bill from the image
steps.description: A billing clerk on the evening shift opens the next image in the queue and types the shipper, consignee, bill-to party, payment terms, pieces, packaging, weight, commodity description, class or dimensions and special instructions such as liftgate or appointment into the TMS freight bill screen.

error.defect_description: Typing error in weight, pieces, postal code or bill-to, or handwriting misread.

evidence.note: Billing clerks need bill of lading experience, 40 wpm typing and ten-key skills; minutes per bill and the evening queue are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Code shipper, consignee and bill-to accounts
steps.description: The clerk searches the customer file by name and postal code to attach existing account codes for the shipper, consignee and the party paying the freight, and picks the correct location when a customer has several. A new consignee is added with the address from the bill.

error.defect_description: Wrong account or wrong bill-to location chosen, which bills the wrong customer.

next.condition: unreadable or missing consignee, bill-to or weight

evidence.note: Handwritten bills often lack a full consignee address or bill-to party; 8% is the author's estimate.

steps.name: Query the terminal about unreadable or missing details
steps.description: The clerk messages or calls the origin terminal service clerk with the PRO number and the missing field, such as an illegible consignee street, a missing weight or no bill-to party on a third-party shipment. The bill is saved on hold so linehaul planning still sees it.

error.defect_description: None introduced; errors pass through.

evidence.note: Author's estimate.

steps.name: Answer the billing query from terminal records
steps.description: The terminal service clerk checks the freight on the dock, the pickup request or the shipper's customer record, or calls the shipper, and replies with the missing detail. Queries raised after the shipper's office closes are answered the next morning.

error.defect_description: Answer is a guess that later proves wrong.

evidence.note: Author's estimate; terminal clerks work extended hours but shippers do not.

steps.name: Check freight class, density and special services
steps.description: The clerk checks the class against the commodity description and, where dimensions are given, the density; flags shipments that are over-length, need an appointment, a liftgate or inside delivery; and enters any collect-on-delivery amount so rating and delivery planning see it.

error.defect_description: Class or density left as the shipper wrote it, or an accessorial not flagged; surfaces later as a reweigh or a disputed charge.

evidence.note: Billing staff classify commodities under the NMFC; NMFTA estimates 70 to 80% of LTL freight is classified by density alone; defect rate is the author's estimate.

steps.name: Flag dangerous goods, cross-border and collect shipments
steps.description: The TMS reads the commodity, destination and service fields and routes bills with dangerous goods, a United States destination or missing customs data to the clerks who handle them. All other bills go straight to release.

error.defect_description: None introduced; errors pass through.

evidence.note: Dangerous goods share of LTL bills (about 4%) and cross-border share (about 3%) are the author's estimates.

steps.name: Check the dangerous goods shipping document
steps.description: The clerk compares the bill with the shipper's dangerous goods shipping document: UN number, shipping name, class, packing group, quantity, the 24-hour emergency number and any ERAP reference, and sets the hazard flags that load planners use to keep incompatible classes apart.
outputs: dangerous goods flags on freight bill

error.defect_description: A class or UN number entered wrongly.

control.basis: Transportation of Dangerous Goods Regulations, Part 3 (shipping document) and Part 1 compatibility rules used in load planning

evidence.note: TDG requirements described from general knowledge; text not opened. Times and shares are the author's estimates.

steps.name: Obtain a corrected dangerous goods document
steps.description: The terminal service clerk tells the dock to hold the freight and calls the shipper for a corrected shipping document. The freight moves only once a complete document is with it and the billing record is updated.

error.defect_description: None introduced; errors pass through.

evidence.note: Author's estimate; shipper contact often waits for the next business morning.

steps.name: Add customs data for United States shipments
steps.description: For a shipment going to the United States, the clerk enters the customs broker, the PAPS barcode number, commodity description and value from the commercial invoice so the cross-border desk can file the ACE manifest before the trailer reaches the border.

error.defect_description: Missing broker or PAPS number, found when the customs desk builds the manifest.

control.basis: US CBP ACE e-Manifest advance data requirement for trucks (filed by the customs desk from the freight bill)

evidence.note: ACE requirement described from general knowledge; text not opened. Times are the author's estimates.

steps.name: Run completeness edits and release the freight bill
steps.description: The TMS runs final edits (duplicate PRO, bill-to present, weight and pieces present) and releases the freight bill so linehaul planners see it on the trailer plan, the destination terminal sees it for delivery and the rating engine can price it. Duplicate or cancelled bills are voided.

error.defect_description: None introduced; errors pass through.

evidence.note: Sample rate and void rate are the author's estimates.

steps.name: Audit a sample of keyed bills against images
steps.description: The billing supervisor opens a random sample of each clerk's bills beside the images and checks every field. Errors are returned to the clerk for correction and counted in the clerk's accuracy score.

error.defect_description: None introduced; errors pass through.

control.basis: Billing department keying accuracy standard and sample audit

evidence.note: Common practice; sample size and error rate are the author's estimates.

steps.name: Match the freight bill to dock loading scans
steps.description: As the dock loads outbound trailers, handheld scans of each PRO label are matched against freight bills. The night report lists freight scanned with no bill and bills whose piece count differs from the pieces scanned.

error.defect_description: None introduced; errors pass through.

evidence.note: Common practice with handheld dock scanning; mismatch share is the author's estimate.

steps.name: Resolve piece-count and PRO mismatches with the dock
steps.description: A billing clerk works the night mismatch report, calling the dock supervisor to recount pieces or read the label, then corrects the freight bill or leaves a note for the overage, shortage and damage clerk when freight is genuinely short or over.

error.defect_description: Bill changed to match a miscount.

evidence.note: Author's estimate.

exceptions.name: Missing bill of lading
exceptions.description: The driver comes back without the signed bill; the terminal asks the shipper for a copy and the bill is keyed next morning.

exceptions.name: Electronic bill fails edits
exceptions.description: The shipper's EDI or portal data has a bad consignee address, no bill-to or no class; a clerk corrects it against the signed image.

exceptions.name: Unreadable or incomplete paper bill
exceptions.description: Handwriting, a missing weight or no bill-to party; the clerk queries the terminal and holds the bill until it answers.

exceptions.name: Dangerous goods document incomplete
exceptions.description: The shipping document lacks a UN number or emergency number; freight is held until the shipper sends a corrected document.

exceptions.name: Piece count does not match dock scans
exceptions.description: The bill says 6 pieces and the dock scanned 5; the clerk and dock supervisor reconcile and refer real shortages to OS&D.

benchmarks.unit: calendar days from the driver handing in paperwork to the freight bill released and matched

evidence.note: A US LTL carrier requires rating finished before a revenue cut-off of about 5 a.m., which means bills keyed the same evening; p50 and p90 are the author's estimates within that window.

benchmarks.population: Paper bills with one or two line items

evidence.note: About 35 bills an hour including lookup and class check; author's estimate from typical data-entry targets.

pain_points.description: Handwritten bills with incomplete consignee or bill-to details cause queries the same night and wrong-party invoices later.

evidence.note: Vendor blog: manual data entry leads to inaccuracies, delays and billing disputes.

pain_points.description: Class and weight are copied as the shipper wrote them; errors surface days later as reweighs and reclassifications that need rebills.

evidence.note: Shippers report up to one in four LTL shipments reweighed or reclassified before they measured freight themselves.

pain_points.description: The evening queue peaks between 18:00 and 22:00 as terminals scan, and Monday and peak-season volume needs overtime to meet the overnight cut-off.

evidence.note: Rating must finish before a daily revenue cut-off of about 5 a.m.

assumptions: About 40% of bills arrive electronically (EDI 211 or customer portal) and 60% only on paper; the signed paper bill is scanned in both cases. The share is the author's estimate for 2019-2022.
Bill entry is done in-house at a central billing centre on an evening shift; some carriers send keying to outsourced data-entry firms, which would change roles and costs but not the steps.

Hands-on time is about 1.7 minutes per bill for billing clerks and about 1.1 minutes for terminal service clerks; this supports about 33 billing clerk FTE on entry, leaving 12 of the organisation file's 45 billing clerks for rating exceptions, where hands-on time implies about 15; the total need of about 48 is slightly above the 45 in the organisation file.
The IT ticket is raised for a whole batch when imaging or EDI fails, a few times a month, not once per bill; the 'any' outcome on that output should be read that way.
The cycle time ignores the hours between signing at the shipper and the driver returning, which belong to pickup execution.
Loaded costs come from the organisation file (wage times 1.30 for hourly staff, 1.35 for salaried).

sources.title: Night Rate Clerk (Roadrunner Freight, Milwaukee) job posting
sources.publisher: Roadrunner Freight, listed on Simplify Jobs
sources.supports: LTL rate clerks use a central auto-rating system to calculate and verify rates on freight bills, hand-rate bills the system cannot rate by applying published pricing agreements and calculating accessorials, process reweighs and inspections from terminals, talk to terminal staff about problem freight bills, help billing staff classify commodities under the NMFC, and finish rating before a daily revenue cut-off of about 5 a.m.; requires experience with bills of lading, freight bills and tariffs and 40 words-per-minute typing and ten-key skills.

sources.title: EDI 211 Motor Carrier Bill of Lading (X12 005010)
sources.supports: The X12 211 transaction lets shippers give a motor carrier a legal bill of lading electronically, with line items for quantity, weight and commodity classification; rates and charges on the bill of lading are subject to audit, and accessorial charges usually cannot be determined until the shipment is delivered, so the 210 invoice is still needed.

sources.title: How Accurate Shipping Data Is Transforming LTL Outcomes
sources.supports: Shippers report that up to one in four LTL shipments came back reweighed or reclassified before they measured freight themselves (one fell to 1% re-rates after using a dimensioner); NMFTA estimates 70 to 80% of LTL freight is classified by density alone; measurements should flow into the bill of lading digitally rather than on paper. Sponsored article promoting one carrier.

sources.title: Common LTL Invoicing Challenges and How to Address Them
sources.supports: Vendor claim, from industry veterans, that 30 to 40% of LTL invoices contain discrepancies, about half from location-related accessorial fees (residential, limited access) and half from reweigh and reclassification; manual data entry leads to inaccuracies, delays and disputes, and auditors may spend an hour on a $10 issue. Year of publication not shown on the page; 2024 is the author's estimate.
